 By  Calvi Leon Staff Reporter 
 Canadian ex-Olympian Ryan Wedding was charged a $100,000 monthly fee to join a secret network of Mexican cartel leaders, gain access to stolen police intelligence and receive alerts on impending arrests as authorities across North America closed in on his cocaine empire, U.S. authorities claim.
 The explosive allegations are contained in an indictment unveiled Tuesday against Edgar Aarón Vazquez , an associate of the Sinaloa Cartel identified as the founder of the New Empire Cartel in Mexico City.
 Known by the aliases “the General” and “Mini,” Vazquez was shot dead last Thursday in what Mexico’s top government security official called an exchange of gunfire with federal police. Secretary  of Security and Citizen Protection Omar García Harfuch said the officers were carrying out a warrant for Vazquez’s arrest on U.S. charges.
 ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW 
 Wedding is accused of running a drug ring that worked with Mexican cartels and ordered multiple murders around the globe — including the mistaken identity killings of an innocent Indian couple in Caledon, Ont., and the assassination of a U.S. federal witness who helped dismantle part of the network.
 Once one of the FBI’s most-wanted fugitives and the subject of a $15-million reward, Wedding was arrested in Mexico in January.
 Vazquez was sanctioned by the U.S. Treasury Department last year over his links to Wedding’s alleged cocaine empire. At the time, the department said Vazquez provided protection for the then-fugitive and used his police contacts to help locate murder targets for the drug ring.
 Edgar Aarón Vazquez Alvarado, or “the General,” was accused or providing protection to ex-Olympian and alleged drug kingpin Ryan Wedding while he was a fugitive in Mexico.
 U.S. Department of Treasury 
 While the circumstances of the takedown remain unclear, the indictment against Vazquez offers the most detailed picture yet of both his role and how Wedding allegedly evaded capture under the protection of some of Mexico’s most notorious criminals.
 According to the indictment, the New Empire Cartel is a violent organization that grew under the protection of “certain Mexican authorities.”
 After his death, Mexican officials described Vazquez as the mastermind behind the high-profile murder of police commissioner Milton Morales Figueroa, head of the Mexico City police’s Tactical Strategy and Special Operations Unit.
 Behind the scenes, the 42-year-old Vazquez allegedly maintained a network of corrupt public officials and private individuals who had access to sensitive information held by Mexican and international law enforcement agencies.
 ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW
 ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW 
 The indictment says he’d sell the information to organized crime leaders who paid subscription-like fees for his services.
 A subscription service for cartel leaders
 According to the indictment, Vazquez charged Wedding a one-time initiation fee of $500,000 (US), followed by an average monthly fee of $100,000.
 For that payment, Vazquez gave up details of ongoing enforcement operations, including arrests, outstanding warrants, active investigations and more, “oftentimes in exchange for an extortionate supplemental fee.”
 The documents do not describe who else paid for Vazquez’s services, but refer to the group as a “collective of organized crime leaders.”
 Live Updates 
 The man who double-crossed Ryan Wedding: The inside story of the life and murder of an FBI witness 
 MONTREAL—The life of a “co-operating witness” is dangerous — especially if you’re double-crossing a drug cartel. 
 Live Updates 
 The man who double-crossed Ryan Wedding: The inside story of the life and murder of an FBI witness 
 MONTREAL—The life of a “co-operating witness” is dangerous — especially if you’re double-crossing a drug cartel. 
 Prosecutors allege Wedding’s organization worked with Mexican drug cartels to move hundreds of kilos of cocaine from Colombia to Mexico at a time via boats and planes. From there, truckers would collect the drugs in stash houses in southern California and elsewhere along the U.S.-Canada border before moving the shipments northward into Canada.
 That trucking network became the focus of a joint investigation by the FBI and RCMP that eventually took down Wedding’s alleged operation.
 ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW
 ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW 
 In Mexico, Vazquez was accused of providing Wedding’s group with “near-daily, rotating code words” for drug couriers to relay to Mexican law enforcement and military personnel at checkpoints, to secure their passage.
 He also gave members of Wedding’s operation authentic law enforcement credentials — altered to bear their names and likenesses — to permit them to pass through Mexican security checkpoints, the indictment alleges. 
 Vazquez paid public officials to slow down criminal investigations and eliminate or manipulate evidence.
 Roberto Gomez, 51, is accused of securing secret police information for Ryan Wedding.
 U.S. Department of Justice 
 Wedding probe growing in scope
 Also Tuesday, U.S. prosecutors unveiled a six-count federal indictment claiming that alleged Los Angeles gangster Roberto Gomez , 51, routinely obtained intelligence about law enforcement operations from Mexican and American authorities before relaying it to Wedding.
 The indictment claims Gomez communicated with leaders of the Sinaloa Cartel and Cártel de Jalisco Nueva Generación (CJNG) and corrupt law enforcement officials to obtain information related to arrests, drug seizures, warrants and charges, then relayed those details to co-conspirators, including Wedding.
 As of Tuesday, a spokesperson at the U.S. Attorney’s Office said Gomez was still at large.
 ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW
 ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW 
 The recent developments reveal an investigation that has expanded greatly in scope since Wedding’s arrest to include allegations of sweeping corruption inside Mexico.
 Vazquez’s death came the same day that U.S. authorities announced the arrest of a Mexican judge for allegedly accepting a $2-million bribe to release Wedding’s Canadian right-hand man from Mexican custody.
 After his arrest in January 2026, Wedding pleaded not guilty to 17 federal felony counts of murder, running a criminal enterprise, drug trafficking and other alleged crimes.
 His lawyer, Anthony Colombo, told the Star in a brief statement on Tuesday that while the latest allegations are “not new,” his client’s plea of not guilty remains. 
 Calvi Leon is a Toronto-based general assignment reporter for
